title: Laras and the Silent Gong
blurb: The big gong has vanished four days before the school show. Laras and Bayu follow the clues.

chapters.title: The Gong Is Gone
chapters.text:
On Monday morning, Laras ran to the music room at her school in Yogyakarta. Monday was her favourite day, because it was gamelan day. The group had to practise for the school show on Friday. Laras could not wait to play the metal bars.

But when she opened the door, she stopped. The drums were there. The metal bars were there. But the big bronze gong was gone, and so was its wooden stand! There was only a clean square on the dusty floor.

Her friend Bayu rushed in behind her. "Did someone take it?" he gasped.

"It is too heavy for one person," said Laras. She frowned. "And the door was locked all weekend."

The other children came in and stood in a quiet group. They all knew that the big gong plays the last deep note of each tune. Without it, the music had no proper ending.

Their teacher, Bu Sari, looked behind the curtain and inside the cupboard. There was no gong. She looked worried. "The show is in four days," she said. "We need that gong."

Laras took a small notebook from her bag. All its pages were clean. "Then we will find it," she said. "I am going to be a detective."

chapters.title: Muddy Clues
chapters.text:
At break time, Laras and Bayu went back to search the room. Bayu looked under the drums. He found a lost pencil and a very old sweet, but no clue. Laras knelt down and studied the floor. Near the clean square, she found a line of dry mud with wide, round marks in it.

"These are not footprints," she said. "They look like wheel marks."

They followed the marks into the corridor, walking slowly with their noses close to the floor. A small boy from Class One laughed at them, but they did not stop. The marks ended at the back door, which was a little open. Bayu pushed it, and hot sun fell on their faces. Outside, more marks crossed the yard towards the old workshop where the caretaker kept his tools.

"Wheels," said Bayu. "Maybe someone used a trolley."

Laras stopped walking. "A trolley can carry something heavy," she said slowly. "So one person could move the gong after all."

She wrote in her notebook: Clue one, wheel marks from the music room to the workshop. Then she noticed something else. On the door handle there was a tiny white petal. She pressed it between two pages and closed the notebook with care.

chapters.title: The Smell of Jasmine
chapters.text:
The workshop door was shut, and a new padlock hung on it. But the children could smell something sweet through the cracks.

"Jasmine," said Laras. She opened her notebook and held up the petal. "The same smell."

Just then, Pak Min the caretaker walked across the yard with a bucket. He always wore a straw hat with a fresh jasmine flower tucked in the band. Every child in the school knew that hat. When he saw Laras and Bayu, he stopped so suddenly that water slopped over his sandals. He looked very nervous.

"Good morning," he said quickly. "I am busy today. Please do not come near the workshop."

He waited until they walked away. When they looked back, he was still standing by the door.

Bayu whispered, "He is hiding something. And he has a key to every door in the school!"

Laras felt a little sick. She liked Pak Min. Last year, he had mended her school bag with strong thread and would not take a single coin for it.

She shook her head slowly. "A clue is not proof," she said. "Many people wear jasmine in Yogyakarta. Let us watch and wait."

"And if he did take it?" asked Bayu.

"Then we will find that out too," said Laras.

chapters.title: A Hum in the Workshop
chapters.text:
At lunchtime, while the others ate rice and fried tempeh, Laras and Bayu crept back towards the workshop.

"We can look," said Laras. "But we do not go inside. That would be wrong."

They stood by the side window, which was a little open. They heard a soft hum, and a tap, tap, tap. Someone was singing a gamelan tune while working.

"That is the tune from our show," Bayu whispered, and he looked puzzled.

He stood on an old box and peeped through the gap. His eyes grew wide. "Laras," he whispered. "I can see the gong! It is standing on a table, and Pak Min is rubbing it with a cloth."

Laras climbed up beside him. The box wobbled. Inside, the air smelled of wood and polish. The gong had always been dull and brown, but now it was shining like gold in the sun. Next to it stood its stand, with pale new wood where there used to be a crack. A trolley with muddy wheels was parked against the wall.

Bayu scratched his head. "Thieves do not polish the things they steal," he whispered. "So why would Pak Min hide it?"

Laras looked down at her notebook. All her clues were in it, but it could not answer that question.

chapters.title: The Surprise
chapters.text:
Laras decided not to guess any more. She climbed off the box, walked round to the front and knocked on the workshop door. Pak Min opened it, and his face went red.

"Oh dear," he said. "You found my secret. I am so sorry. I should have left a note."

He gave them a stool each and explained everything. Last week he saw a crack in the wooden stand. He was afraid that the heavy gong would fall during the show. So on Saturday, he came in with his keys. He rolled the gong and the stand on a trolley to the workshop. It had rained that day, so the wheels carried mud from the yard into the music room. Then he mended the stand and polished the bronze.

"I wanted to give Bu Sari a surprise," he said. "She works so hard."

"We thought you were a thief," said Laras in a small voice.

Pak Min laughed until his hat slipped. "A good detective wonders," he said. "Next time, come and ask me."

That afternoon, they pushed the gong back to the music room. Bu Sari clapped her hands. On Friday, the gong's deep note rolled through the hall at the end of each tune. Laras wrote one last line in her notebook: Case closed. Ask first, guess later.
